To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we developed a network model of working memory that can be used to predict the behavioral effects of cortical disinhibition.

1) a model of prefrontal cortical microcircuit dysfunction, via disinhibition, predicts increased behavioral variability and impaired ability to filter out irrelevant information in spatial working memory, and 2) these behavioral deficits are observed in human subjects performing spatial working memory under ketamine infusion, an NMDA receptor antagonist that disrupts E/I balance.

1) cortical disinhibition leads to broadening of the tuning of WM-selective persistent activity and 2) broadened persistent activity degrades the ability of the WM network to maintain information with high precision and filter out distractors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how neural circuits in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) support working memory (WM), a process by which the brain maintains a representation of information for use in future decisions or behaviors.
the mechanisms by which neural circuits process information.
how the brain represents and stores information in working memory (WM) and how this process is disrupted in schizophrenia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model provides a mechanistic explanation of the effects of disinhibition on working memory.
this work demonstrates a specific way in which cortical disinhibition may contribute to the cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.
the model predicts that cortical disinhibition will increase behavioral variability, decrease the precision of stored WM information, and decrease distractor filtering during WM maintenance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a computational model of spatial working-memory, and we have used this model to investigate the effects of disinhibition on working-memory function.
we have identified the neural and behavioral signatures of disinhibition, a core deficit of schizophrenia, and have proposed a mechanism for how it affects cognitive function.

we have developed a model of spatial working (short-term) memory (STM) in prefrontal cortices, and that this model predicts that schizophrenia-related disinhibition of excitatory pyramidal neurons leads to increased variability in spatial STM.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a model that captures the microcircuit dysfunction of schizophrenia can predict behavioral impairments and suggest compensatory mechanisms.
the effects of cortical disinhibition on WM can be understood by examining changes in E/I balance at the microcircuitry level.

a model of schizophrenia that is based on a single, well-studied mechanism (NMDA receptor hypofunction) can explain multiple aspects of the disease (cognitive impairment, hallucinations, and negative symptoms).
